title: The Stockout Surge

scenario.situation: Stockout incidents rose 40% last quarter, triggering customer complaints and lost revenue.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The Ops VP is convinced the whole catalogue is under-buffered and wants to raise safety stock levels across every SKU immediately.
scenario.question: Is the stockout surge a catalogue-wide inventory problem, or is something more specific going on?

decisions.prompt: The Ops VP wants you to model how much safety stock to add across the catalogue. How do you frame your investigation?

options.label: Model optimal safety stock levels for all SKUs
options.detail: Use demand variability and lead-time data to recalculate safety stock thresholds catalogue-wide.
options.consequence: You produce a clean model, but it assumes the problem is uniform. You've answered a question the data never validated — and the VP's assumption is baked into your output from step one.
options.divergenceCost: Accepted the stakeholder's framing uncritically and optimized before diagnosing.

options.label: Diagnostic concentration analysis
options.detail: Before prescribing a fix, segment stockouts by SKU, category, and supplier to see where they actually concentrate.
options.consequence: You map stockouts across the catalogue and immediately see they are not uniform — a handful of SKUs account for the vast majority of incidents. The investigation now has a real thread to pull.

options.label: Compare this quarter to prior quarters for each category
options.detail: Look at stockout trend lines by product category to spot which categories worsened most.
options.consequence: Trends by category smooth over SKU-level spikes. You see a few categories look worse, but you can't tell whether it's one bad SKU dragging the category or a broad problem — the signal is still aggregated.
options.divergenceCost: Aggregated at the category level, masking the true concentration at the SKU and supplier level.

options.label: Survey warehouse ops staff about fulfillment pain points
options.detail: Talk to the team closest to the problem to gather qualitative explanations.
options.consequence: Staff surface anecdotes about a few problem products, but without data to back it up you can't quantify the impact or convince the VP. Useful color, not the answer.
options.divergenceCost: Chose a slow, anecdotal instrument when the pattern was already in the stockout records.

decisions.prompt: Your segmentation reveals stockout incidents are not spread evenly. Which metric do you use to confirm where the real problem lives?

artifact.title: Stockout incidents by SKU group — this quarter (raw counts)
artifact.caption: Raw incident counts across SKU groups. SKUs 1–3 look large, but could they just have higher sales volume?

options.label: Raw stockout incident counts by SKU group
options.detail: Rank SKU groups by total number of stockout events this quarter.
options.consequence: SKUs 1–3 do show the most incidents in absolute terms — but high-volume SKUs naturally have more exposure. You can't tell if this is a rate problem or just a size effect, and the VP can push back.
options.divergenceCost: Used raw counts that don't control for sales volume — conflated exposure with risk.

options.label: Stockout rate AND supplier lead-time deviation by SKU group
options.detail: Calculate stockouts per 100 order-days for each group, then cross-reference with supplier lead-time data to see if the concentration maps to a single supply source.
options.consequence: Normalized for volume, SKUs 1–3 have a stockout rate 11× the catalogue average — and all three share the one supplier whose lead time blew out by 18 days this quarter. The rest of the catalogue is statistically unremarkable.

artifact.title: Stockout rate (per 100 order-days) by SKU group — this quarter
artifact.caption: Normalized for volume, SKUs 1–3 are clear outliers at 34.2 — all three share the supplier whose lead time extended 18 days. The rest of the catalogue clusters near 3.0.

decisions.prompt: SKUs 1–3, all from the same supplier with a blown-out lead time, account for roughly 80% of the stockout surge. What do you tell the Ops VP?

options.label: "It's the supplier's lead time — cancel the blanket restock and fix that one relationship."
options.detail: Make the causal call and recommend a targeted supplier action only.
options.consequence: You've correctly identified the concentration, but asserting causation without a controlled comparison leaves you exposed. The lead-time blowout and stockouts are correlated; a confounding factor — like a demand spike on those three SKUs — could be co-driving the result.
options.divergenceCost: Overclaimed causation from correlation, skipping the step needed to rule out confounders.

options.label: "The data doesn't support a blanket restock — 80% of incidents trace to 3 SKUs sharing one supplier whose lead time extended sharply. That's the priority. Before committing capital, let's verify by pulling the demand signal on those SKUs and confirming lead-time records with the supplier."
options.detail: Present the concentration finding, flag the causal gap, and propose a targeted next step before acting.
options.consequence: You've reframed the VP's assumption with hard evidence, protected the company from unnecessary capital lock-up, and defined a clear, fast path to causal confirmation. That's the full analyst job.

insight: The 40% stockout surge was not a catalogue-wide buffering failure — roughly 80% of incidents were concentrated in just three SKUs tied to a single supplier whose lead time extended significantly. A blanket safety-stock increase would have locked up capital across hundreds of SKUs to solve a problem that lived in three. The core lesson is Pareto thinking applied to operations: always disaggregate before prescribing, because aggregate metrics routinely hide the concentration that makes the real fix cheap and targeted.
